Not an ICMP ping: cardano-cli ping opens a TCP connection and runs the node-to-node handshake, so each sample is an application-level round trip through both nodes' network stacks and mux, which is what the Cardano protocols actually experience. The TCP connect column is the bare TCP round trip from the same tool, the closest stand-in for a raw ping. SEM = SD / sqrt(n). The spread is 412x, from 0.61 ms within AP to 250.41 ms between AP and EU, and it is the floor under every interval in this report.

tx-centrifuge

The load generator, a closed-loop driver. A workload is a self-contained circuit: its own disjoint partition of funds, single-use UTxOs, its own builder turning funds into transactions, its own token-bucket rate limit, its own injection targets and its own observer following the chain. Every transaction spends funds and creates outputs, and an output becomes spendable again only once that workload's observer has seen its transaction reach the confirmation depth, so the transactions form chains gated by the chain itself and the funds budget is the buffer bridging confirmation latency. With on_exhaustion = error the generator fails the run the moment a node asks for transactions and it has none to hand over, whatever left it empty: too small an initial budget, funds not coming back from confirmation, a builder that cannot keep pace, or simply a target pulling faster than the loop can refill. It is one guard against the whole class of not keeping up, and it is loud rather than a quiet slowdown.

  • 51 workloads and 51 observers, one of each per pool: every workload drives its own pool and no other (51 of 51), and its observer follows that same pool rather than a shared one (51 of 51)
  • builder value, every transaction 2-in 2-out with 2 destination signing key per builder, fee 1,000,000
  • rate limit: token_bucket, scope per_target, at 3.28 tx/s per target, 167.1 tx/s offered in aggregate (62.48 KB/s at the 374 B measured transaction size)
  • recycling on_confirm at confirmation depth 3, over a nodetonode observer
  • initial funds from genesis-funds (genesis_utxo_keys), scope per_workload, so a fund returned by a workload can only be taken up by that same workload
  • on_exhaustion = error · max_batch_size = 0

The generator runs on its own machine in eu-central-1, which forges nothing, so every transaction crosses the network before the pool that must place it in a block ever sees it: the round trip a workload pays is the EU row for its target's region in the table above. Each workload holds two buffers of its own, funds waiting to be built and built transactions waiting to be delivered.

Endorser block contents

What an endorser block holds. An endorser block is a list of (tx hash, size) references and nothing else, so its size is that list's size.

The transaction closure is what binds this run. Its transactions are 374 B each, so its largest endorser block holds 2,673 of them: 98,904 B of references against the 100,000 B cap (98.9%), and 999,702 B of transactions against the 1,000,000 B the closure allows (100.0%). The one that reaches 100% is the one that stopped the endorser block from growing.

The other run of this pair, 2026-11-09-16-29-2a1ad-w45ezenotxsu-value-leios-workload-all-n2n-100k1m-2i2o2w-nomadperf-dira-nom, is the control for exactly this: its transactions are 374 B, its largest endorser block holds 2,673 references for 98,904 B (98.9% of the reference cap), and their closure is 999,702 B (100.0% of the closure cap). With 374 B transactions the closure fills first, with 374 B transactions the closure does, off the same two caps. So the same cap binds in both, and the transaction size did not move it.

1.2. Start Leadership Check

A slot's start is fixed by the protocol, the system start plus the slot length, and everything here is measured against it. A node traces every slot it enters, so a slot with no trace is one it never entered, and each node is counted over its own window, from the first slot it entered to its last.

Forging in the slot

One value per block, from the start of its own slot to its forging: every ranking block in the first row, every forging that carries an endorser block in the second, so a hash forged twice counts twice. Section 6 measures that second stage again from the same origin but counts each hash once, at its first forging, which is why its samples are fewer.

2. Propagation, fetching the EB references

Three instants are used:

  • The forger forges the endorser block (Consensus.LeiosKernel.BlockForged)
  • The forger announces it over the network (LeiosNotify.Remote.Send.BlockAnnouncement)
  • A peer finishes receiving the endorser block's bytes over the network (LeiosFetch.Remote.Receive.Block)

Where an endorser block's hash was forged more than once, and so referenced by more than one ranking block, the first forging is the one used and the later ones are ignored: the instants this section reads are the first for that hash and node, so they belong to the first forging.

The forger alone: from forging the endorser block to sending its first announcement of it.

3. Acquiring, the EB written down

A delivered endorser block is not yet held: until its write is durable the body still reads as not-held, which is why the same endorser block can be fetched again meanwhile. Consensus.LeiosKernel.BlockAcquired is the moment that ends: the node has the reference list stored and claims to hold it, registering which referenced transactions it still needs. This is the step from arrival to that claim, which includes waiting for the single writer, and how often the same endorser block was stored again.

4. Closures, the transactions an EB references

An endorser block is a list of references. The transactions themselves are a separate transfer, and a node has the closure once it holds all of them: Consensus.LeiosKernel.BlockTxsAcquired. Counted per peer and endorser block, on the same endorser blocks as sections 2 and 3.

5. Certifying

5.1. Totals

Counted on the blocks the whole cluster took. A block qualifies when all 50 nodes other than its forger adopted it, every peer it has of the 51 in the cluster: 3,174 of the run's 3,291 walkable blocks. Both sides of the ratio are held to it, so an announcement made by a block only part of the cluster held, and a certificate carried by one, are both out. No battle or fork filter is applied: nothing here asks what happened at a contested height. The blocks come from every forging the logs can place on a chain, both sides of a fork included, and the test above is adoption by every peer, not having won the height.

5.2. What happened to every endorser block

Hover a stage for what it counts and which trace says so. The stages down to Never reached quorum count endorser blocks; the rows under it count voter decisions, one per trace event, which is why they sum past 100%. Nothing is gated here, not even the run's opening epochs: every endorser block any ranking block announced is counted, which is why this table is wider than the cards above. 117 endorser blocks were announced only by blocks that part of the cluster never adopted, and the two carried counts differ by 0, certificates whose carrier was not adopted by every peer. tooLate is the voter's own refusal, counted once per voter and endorser block and only on the ones that never reached quorum: a node logs it when the window had already shut before it began, whether or not it ever held the transactions, so it is not section 4's late closures.

7. Forks

Every time a node abandoned a chain it already had for a better one, counted once for each node that did it (ChainDB.AddBlockEvent.SwitchedToAFork). A contest is one pair of tips, so a contest the whole cluster lived through counts once. Both rates below are contests per 1,000 blocks on the chain, so runs of different length compare directly.

The slot rate is the control and the height rate is the signal: two leaders in one slot is fixed by activeSlotsCoeff and cannot be engineered away, while a height battle is a node forging on a parent a sibling already had, which is propagation losing a race and is free to move. Reading the height rate without the control beside it cannot tell a propagation regression from a run that simply drew more forks.
